title: 16 Hours of OPTIMJACK. Now Picture Black Friday.
summary: One compromised testing script reached 178 organizations in a single day. What OPTIMJACK's 16 hours would have cost on Black Friday, and how to stop trusted scripts that turn malicious.
body_markdown:
*One compromised testing script reached 178 organizations in a single day. On the biggest shopping day of the year, the same attack would hit at peak traffic.*


**The short version:** On Sunday, November 16, an attacker abused a flaw in a widely used A/B testing platform and planted malicious code in customer projects. For roughly 16 hours, that code ran on the websites of 178 organizations, served from the vendor's own CDN under the vendor's own certificate. It skimmed payment cards, swapped cryptocurrency addresses and targeted iPhone and iPad visitors with exploit kits. Researchers named it[OPTIMJACK](https://www.feroot.com/blog/optimizely-breach-third-party-supply-chain-attacks/) . Black Friday is the day to ask what those 16 hours would have cost at peak traffic.


## How the 16 hours unfolded


According to researcher timelines reported by[SecureWorld](https://www.secureworld.io/industry-news/third-party-script-hijack-optimjack) , the first malicious code appeared early on November 16. Over the next 16 hours or so, the attacker rebuilt the payload 26 times, adding features and destination wallets as the day went on, and added real-time card skimming partway through. Researchers who checked 1,611 of the vendor's hosted files found 188 infected snippets across 178 organizations in 20 sectors. The vendor fixed the flaw and removed the code early on November 17.


None of the affected organizations deployed anything. They didn't push a release, change a line of code or receive a warning. They had approved a vendor once, and the vendor's code changed underneath them.


## Why the usual defenses waved it through


Every control built around trusting a vendor's domain let OPTIMJACK in. The code came from the right CDN, with a valid certificate, through a script tag the security team had approved. Content Security Policy allowlists, vendor reviews and annual assessments all treat that as safe. Server patching and network monitoring never saw it, because the code ran in the customer's browser and on the customer's phone. Days earlier,[PaperCut](https://www.feroot.com/blog/papercut-newspaper-card-skimmer-supply-chain-attacks/) went further on about 80 newspaper checkouts, hiding inside a payment processor's own card form and sending stolen cards out over WebRTC, a channel Content Security Policy doesn't control.


That is the client-side gap in a single example. Attackers using AI can build, test and rebuild a payload 26 times in a day. A defense that checks scripts once a quarter is working on a different clock.


## Now picture it on Black Friday


OPTIMJACK started on a Sunday in mid-November. Moved to Black Friday morning, the same 16 hours would cover the heaviest checkout traffic of the year, with change freezes in place and teams focused on keeping sites up. A skimmer live for a day can collect card data from every shopper who reaches checkout before anyone notices, and the first alert often comes weeks later from a card brand.


## Watching behavior, not just the source


Stopping an attack like OPTIMJACK means judging every script by what it does, whoever it comes from.
